To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dietary carbohydrate and fat alter the nitrogen metabolism and the hepatic gluconeogenic activity in rats.
the low carbohydrate-high fat diets cause reduction of urea production and enhancement of glucose production at the fixed level of dietary protein in weanling and in growing rats.
a high fat-low carbohydrate diet enhances hepatic gluconeogenic enzyme activities in both weanling rats and growing rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of dietary carbohydrates and fats on the protein and carbohydrate metabolism in weanling and in growing rats.
the effect of dietary fat on protein utilization.
the effect of dietary carbohydrates on the regulation of hepatic gluconeogenic and ureogenic enzymes in the weanlings and growing rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a low carbohydrate diet is more suitable for the growing rats.

the alteration of dietary proportions of carbohydrate and lipid in a fixed protein diet does not alter the protein metabolism but does affect the carbohydrate metabolism in weanling and in growing rats.
the alteration of the proportions of carbohydrate to fat in the diets does not affect the growth rate, but does affect protein metabolism and the activities of ureogenic and glucoeogenic enzymes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the low carbohydrate-high fat diets may be beneficial to the growing rats in terms of growth rate and nitrogen retention.

in the weanlings, the 50% carbohydrate-30% fat diet is optimal for the protein and carbohydrate metabolism, and in the growing rats, the 30% and the 50% fat diets are the optimal diets for protein and carbohydrate metabolism.
the dietary carbohydrate and fat affect the nitrogen metabolism by changing the urea and glucose metabolism in the liver.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dietary composition affects the metabolic pathways of the body.
a high fat diet can be used as a therapeutic approach to reduce the uremic burden in patients with chronic kidney disease.
the alteration in the proportion of carbohydrate and fat does not affect growth rate but does affect the protein and carbohydrate metabolism in weanling and in growing rats.
